title: Man. Post. Cap. VI: GAR 1 Augustine/Martyr; PLAC — divine act not answered
pass_a_gloss: GAR Reply 1: 'all were one man in Adam' is not new invention but old Catholic doctrine, especially Augustine against the Pelagians, often restated. One citation may do—Epistle 106 to Boniface: those who would be many in themselves from that one were one man in him. Ask Augustine his source and he points to the Apostle's witness that all sinned in Adam; they sinned in Adam, so they were one in Adam. Martyr, among the gravest theologians the learned man cites, marked the same when he wrote that Adam's fall was as if all had stood present and fallen with him. PLAC: the reply misses my question. I did not ask for a source that men were somehow one in Adam; I asked for a source that God so regarded them as one that He immediately charged them with Adam's first actual sin. That divine inward act was the issue—and this answer says nothing about it.
pass_b_english: GAR. Response 1. That all men were one man in Adam is not a recent fiction, but the old doctrine of the Catholics, and namely of Augustine disputing against the Pelagians, which he often repeats in his works. Let one place from Epistle 106 to Boniface suffice for now: Whoever from that one were to be many in themselves were one man in him. If you ask Augustine whence he has it, he will answer that he has it from the Apostle, where he testifies that all sinned in Adam. They sinned in Adam: therefore they were one in Adam. Which Martyr also, one of the weightiest theologians whose authority the learned man urges in this matter, clearly signified when he wrote that Adam's sinning was the same as if all had been present and had sinned with Adam. PLAC. He answers something other than I asked. For I did not ask whence he had it that all men were one man in Adam, but whence he had it that God had considered all men as one man in Adam, so that He immediately imputed to them that first actual sin of Adam. The debate was about that consideration, about that inner act of the divine mind—on which, however, there is deep silence in this reply.
source_text: GAR. Respons. 1. omnes homines fuisse unum hominem in Adamo, non commentum recens est, sed vetus Catholicorum, ac nominatim Augustini adversus Pelagianos disputantis doctrina, quam saepius in operibus suis repetit. Sufficiat nunc unus ille locus ex Epist. 106. ad Bonifac. Quicunque ex illo uno multi in seipsis futuri erant, in illo unus homo erant. Si ab Augustino quaeras, unde id habeat, respondebit ex Apostolo se habere, ubi testatur omnes in Adamo peccasse. In Adamo peccarunt: itaque unum fuerunt in Adamo. Quod & Martyr, unus ex gravissimis Theologis, quorum auctoritatem obtendit in hoc negotio vir doctus, evidenter significavit ubi scripsit, Adamo peccante idem fuisse, ac si omnes praesentes fuissent, & cum Adamo peccavissent. PLAC. Aliud quaesivi, aliud respondet. Non enim quaesivi, unde haberet, omnes homines fuisse unum hominem in Adamo; sed unde haberet, Deum considerasse omnes homines tanquam unum hominem in Adamo, ita ut illis primum illud peccatum actuale Adami imputaverit immediate? De illa consideratione, de illo interno mentis divinae actu agebatur: de quo tamen altum in hac responsione silentium.

lemmas.gloss: that God considered ... and immediately imputed

choices.choice: Augustine/Martyr prove human unity, not God's immediate-imputing act
